isaac.text: Blindness in old age appears three times in the Old Testament, with Isaac, Eli and Ahijah, and the 1915 Bible encyclopedia thought cataract the likely cause in each case. That is a physician's guess from a century ago; the text itself gives no cause. The same entry notes that an Egyptian medical text of about 1500 BC already listed many eye diseases and a hundred prescriptions for them, so failing eyes were a familiar part of life in Isaac's world.

Josephus, retelling the story in the first century, has Jacob wear a goat's skin on his arm so that its hairy roughness would persuade his father he was Esau. He also has Isaac explain that his blindness and great age kept him from offering sacrifice, which is why he asked for the meal before giving the blessing. Those details are Josephus's additions to Genesis.
isaac.source: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews (Whiston translation), Book I, chapter 18.

isaac.text: What was at stake was more than a father's good wishes. The 1915 encyclopedia explains that when Isaac blessed Jacob he spoke as if in God's place, so that the blessing was part prayer and part prediction of the good named in it. That is why it could not simply be taken back when the deception came out.

jacob.text: Jacob's last years were spent in Goshen, on the eastern edge of the Nile delta, which Smith's dictionary describes as pasture land suited to a shepherd people, where the Israelites prospered and kept somewhat apart from the Egyptians. Genesis 47:27 places the family there. So the blessing in Genesis 48 is given by an old shepherd in a foreign land, far from the places where his own story had happened.
jacob.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entry "Goshen"; Genesis 47:27.

jacob.text: Matthew Henry, writing around 1710, noticed that Jacob was dim-sighted in old age just as his father had been, and drew the lesson that "the eye of faith may be very clear even when the eye of the body is very much clouded." That is a preacher's observation rather than history, but it is the oldest comment on the shelf about Jacob's eyes, and it matches what the passage shows.
jacob.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1721), on Genesis 48.

eli.text: Shiloh, where Eli served, lay in the hill country of Ephraim north of Bethel, east of the road from Bethel to Shechem. Smith's dictionary calls it one of the earliest and most sacred Hebrew sanctuaries: the ark was kept there from the last days of Joshua until Samuel's time. After the ark was lost in the battle that killed Eli, Shiloh "sank into insignificance."

Eli was a descendant of Aaron through his son Ithamar and, according to Smith's, the first of that line to serve as high priest. He was also Israel's judge, which the Bible says he had been for forty years when he died at ninety-eight.
eli.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entry "Eli"; 1 Samuel 4:18.

eli.text: Josephus tells Eli's death in a sentence: when he heard that the ark had been taken, he fell from his seat and died, having lived ninety-eight years and governed for forty. Josephus does not mention his eyes.
eli.source: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews (Whiston translation), Book V, chapter 11.

ahijah.text: Ahijah was the prophet who, years earlier, met Jeroboam on the road out of Jerusalem, tore a new garment into twelve pieces and gave him ten, as a sign that he would rule ten tribes. Josephus retells that scene and says it happened in a quiet place off the road. The blind old man at the door in 1 Kings 14 is the same prophet who had once announced the king's rise.
ahijah.source: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews (Whiston translation), Book VIII, chapter 7; compare 1 Kings 11:29-31.

ahijah.text: The queen travelled from Tirzah, Jeroboam's royal city in the hills north of Shechem, which Smith's describes as a city famous for its beauty, to Shiloh, the old sanctuary town in the hills of Ephraim. The shelf gives no distance between them, so the length of her journey cannot be stated.
ahijah.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entries "Tirzah" and "Shiloh."

ahijah.text: Josephus tells the story with the same facts as the Bible: the queen changed her clothes, Ahijah's eyes were dim with age, God told him who was coming, and he called out to her before she had come in. The 1915 encyclopedia lists Ahijah with Isaac and Eli as a case of blindness in old age.
ahijah.source: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews (Whiston translation), Book VIII, chapter 11; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915), entry "Blindness."

samson.text: Gaza, where Samson was imprisoned, was one of the five chief Philistine cities, the last town in the south-west of the land on the road toward Egypt. Its name means "the strong." Smith's notes that it had deep wells of excellent water and a long history as a military stronghold.

Both Smith's and Josephus dwell on the moment Samson asked to be led to the pillars. Josephus adds that Samson told the boy who led him by the hand that he was weary and wanted to lean on them, a detail not in the Bible. The servant who guided a blind prisoner to his place became, without knowing it, the means of what followed.
samson.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entry "Samson"; Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews (Whiston translation), Book V, chapter 8.

samson.text: Grinding grain was usually women's work, done with a hand mill of two round stones about a foot and a half across, the upper turned by a handle while the worker sat on the ground. Smith's describes the mills still in use in the 1860s and says the ancient ones probably differed little. Whether Samson turned a hand mill or something larger, the Bible does not say; either way, the strongest man in Israel was set to the most ordinary and repetitive labour there was.
samson.caution: Smith's describes 19th-century mills and does not mention Samson.

zedekiah.text: Smith's traces the king's flight: when the wall was breached at midnight he left by the gate on the opposite side with his household and took the road toward the Jordan. At dawn the pursuers caught him near Jericho and carried him north to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, at the upper end of the valley of Lebanon. There his sons were killed before him and his eyes put out.

Josephus points out that two prophecies met in this one act. Jeremiah had said Zedekiah would see the king of Babylon face to face and be taken there; Ezekiel had said he would not see Babylon. Both came true: he stood before Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, and he arrived in Babylon blind.
zedekiah.source: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews (Whiston translation), Book X, chapter 8; compare Jeremiah 34:3 and Ezekiel 12:13.

zedekiah.text: Smith's notes that blinding on purpose, for political ends, is alluded to in Scripture, and gives two cases: Nahash's threat at Jabesh-gilead and Zedekiah here. It was a known instrument of conquerors.

men-of-sodom.text: Smith's sets Sodom as the chief of four cities in the plain of the Jordan, which from the hills near Bethel looked like one great oasis, "a garden of Jehovah," with the cities standing in the middle of it. That is the view before the destruction, as Genesis 13 describes it.

Josephus describes the city of Lot's day as grown proud on its riches, unjust toward men and impious toward God, and says its people "hated strangers." The night at Lot's door is, in his telling, a rich city's hostility to two visitors.
men-of-sodom.source: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews (Whiston translation), Book I, chapter 11.

aramean-raiders.text: Dothan, where Elisha was staying, is first mentioned in the story of Joseph. An early Christian writer placed it twelve miles north of Samaria, and the site was found in the 19th century still bearing its ancient name. Samaria, the capital Elisha led the soldiers to, stood on a hill in a wide valley about thirty miles north of Jerusalem.
aramean-raiders.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entries "Dothan" and "Samaria."
aramean-raiders.caution: The twelve miles is an ancient writer's figure as Smith's reports it.

aramean-raiders.text: Josephus retells the night: the Syrian king sent a great army with horses and chariots to surround Dothan, and Elisha prayed that God would dim the enemies' eyes and cast a mist before them. In his words they were so darkened in sight and in mind that they followed Elisha diligently all the way to Samaria, where the king of Israel was told to shut the gates behind them.
aramean-raiders.source: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews (Whiston translation), Book IX, chapter 4.

aramean-raiders.text: Josephus gives the sequel in the same chapter. Elisha argued that these men had done the land no harm and had come "without knowing it, by the Divine Power," so the king feasted them splendidly and sent them home. The war between Damascus and Samaria went on, but these raiders did not come back.
aramean-raiders.source: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews (Whiston translation), Book IX, chapter 4; compare 2 Kings 6:23.

saul-on-the-damascus-road.text: Damascus lay about 130 miles north-east of Jerusalem, in Smith's words, in a plain of great size and fertility on the edge of the desert, and had always been a centre of trade. Saul set out on a long road to a rich and busy city, and arrived in it unable to see.
saul-on-the-damascus-road.caution: Smith's distance is a straight-line figure from the 1860s.

saul-on-the-damascus-road.text: Visitors to Damascus have long been shown a street called Straight, running through the city from east to west, and the houses of Judas and Ananias. Smith's, in the 1860s, allowed that the street may be the one in Acts but said little confidence could be placed in the house traditions. Where Saul sat in the dark for three days is not known.

A physician writing in the 1915 encyclopedia thought Saul's blindness was a temporary paralysis of the retina from the brightness of the light, that the "scales" were how it felt rather than a thing that fell, and that his eyes may have stayed weak afterwards. That is one doctor's opinion from a century ago, stated more confidently than the text allows, and the Bible gives no diagnosis.
saul-on-the-damascus-road.caution: A 1915 medical opinion; shown as such.

elymas.text: Cyprus is an island about 140 miles long with two chief cities in Paul's day: Salamis at the east end, where he and Barnabas landed, and Paphos at the west end, where they met the proconsul. They crossed the whole island between the two.
elymas.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entries "Cyprus" and "Paphos"; Acts 13:5-6.

elymas.text: Paphos was famous across the ancient world for the worship of Aphrodite, whose temple stood at the old town while the harbour and government were at the new town ten miles off. A Jewish sorcerer serving a Roman governor in a city of Aphrodite is the setting of this story.
elymas.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entries "Paphos" and "Cyprus."

elymas.text: Smith's describes Sergius Paulus as an intelligent, truth-seeking man eager for information from every source within reach, which is why both a magician and two travelling preachers had his ear. It gives Elymas as an Arabic name meaning "wise man," the title the sorcerer Bar-Jesus went by.
elymas.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entries "Sergius Paulus" and "Elymas."

two-blind-men.text: Edersheim places this healing on the way back to Capernaum after the raising of the synagogue leader's daughter, and is careful to separate it from the similar healing in Matthew 12, which he says came much later. Elsewhere, though, he wonders whether the details point to a setting away from Galilee, and he does not settle the question. The place is uncertain.
two-blind-men.source: Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book III, chapters XXII and XXXIV.

two-blind-men.text: Matthew Henry pictures the two men following Jesus through the streets "as beggars do, with their incessant cries," and notes that "Son of David" was the common name for the Messiah. They were not asking a healer for help; they were naming who they believed He was.
two-blind-men.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1721), on Matthew 9.

two-blind-men.text: Why tell them to keep it quiet? Edersheim suggests that a profession of faith as far-reaching as theirs, calling Him Son of David and able to open blind eyes by a touch, was not yet to be proclaimed in public. That is his reading. The men did not keep quiet.
two-blind-men.source: Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book III, chapter XXXIV.

blind-and-mute-man.text: Edersheim keeps this healing apart from the one in Matthew 9. This one, told also in Luke 11, came at a much later point, when opposition had hardened and the charge that Jesus worked by the prince of demons had taken shape. That explains why the healing itself gets one verse and the argument gets the rest of the chapter.
blind-and-mute-man.source: Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book III, chapter XXII.

blind-and-mute-man.text: Eye disease in the ancient Near East was widely thought to be a divine infliction, the 1915 encyclopedia says, citing Exodus 4:11. That is a statement about how blindness was understood in general. Matthew gives no cause for this man's condition beyond the spirit that held him.

bethsaida.text: Bethsaida was a fishing town; the name means "house of fish," and it was the home of Andrew, Peter and Philip. Excavations at the candidate sites on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee have turned up fishing weights and net-mending needles. Which ruin is the Bethsaida of the Gospels is still argued.
bethsaida.source: Wikipedia, "Bethsaida," revision of 18 July 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0); Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entry "Bethsaida."

bethsaida.text: Edersheim calls this the only gradual cure in the Gospels and notes that saliva was a well-known Jewish remedy for the eyes. He infers from the man's words about trees that the blindness was not from birth but the result of disease. That inference is his, not the text's, though the man's knowledge of what trees look like points the same way.
bethsaida.source: Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book III, chapter XXXIV.

bartimaeus.text: The Jericho Bartimaeus knew was the City of Palms, about six hours' walk from Jerusalem and the first stop for pilgrims going up to Passover. Springs and aqueducts watered a rich plain, and its streets held, in Edersheim's picture, pilgrims from Galilee and beyond the Jordan, priests, traders and the traffic of the caravan road from Arabia and Damascus. It was also the central station for collecting taxes, which is why Zacchaeus lived there.
bartimaeus.source: Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book IV, chapter XXIV.

bartimaeus.text: Herod's successor Archelaus brought water to the plain and planted it with palms, so that, in Smith's words, "Jericho was once more a city of palms when our Lord visited it." Josephus calls it the most fruitful country in Judea, with its palms and its balsam trees, whose sap was gathered as it dripped "like tears." A blind man sitting by that road would have known it by its sounds and its smells.
bartimaeus.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entry "Jericho"; Josephus, The Wars of the Jews (Whiston translation), Book I, chapter 6.

bartimaeus.text: Jericho lies in the Jordan Valley some 250 metres below sea level, the lowest city in the world, and in this period it held palaces and a winter resort for Jerusalem's wealthy. From it, the road to Jerusalem climbs about a thousand metres. Jesus and the crowd were about to begin that climb.
bartimaeus.caution: Modern figures; Second Temple Jericho stood a few kilometres from the modern town.

bartimaeus.text: Smith's says that in later times beggars had fixed places, at street corners, at the Temple gates or at the gates of houses, and cites this very verse. Those unable to work through bodily infirmity were usually cared for by their relatives, so a man begging by the road may have had no one.
bartimaeus.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entries "Bartimaeus" and "Beggar, Begging."

bartimaeus.text: The three Gospels do not agree on whether this happened as Jesus entered Jericho or as He left, and Matthew has two men where Mark and Luke have one. Edersheim suggests Bartimaeus was the spokesman of two, and on the other difference he says plainly that it is better to admit the problem than to force a harmony. Bartimaeus is one of very few people healed in the Gospels whose name is recorded.
bartimaeus.source: Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book IV, chapter XXIV; Wikipedia, "Healing the blind near Jericho," revision of 16 August 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0).

the-temple.text: The outer court of Herod's Temple, the Court of the Gentiles, worked as a market. Edersheim describes the official money-changers who, for a fee, turned foreign coins into the coin the Temple accepted, and "that great mart for sacrificial animals." Herod had doubled the size of the Temple Mount, to about fourteen hectares, and its porches were where this business was done.
the-temple.source: Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book II, chapter I; Wikipedia, "Second Temple," revision of 19 September 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0).

the-temple.text: As the traders were driven out, Edersheim pictures the blind and the lame coming in "from porches and Temple-Mount" to be healed, and the children taking up the shout of Hosanna. He guesses the children may have been sons of the Levites who sang in the Temple.
the-temple.source: Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book V, chapter II.

the-temple.text: Matthew Henry set this scene against 2 Samuel 5:8: the blind and the lame had been shut out of David's palace, and here they were received in God's house. The Temple, he said, was profaned when made a market and honoured when made a hospital.
the-temple.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1721), on Matthew 21.

the-temple.text: Under the Law a blind descendant of Aaron could not serve at the altar (Leviticus 21:18), though he was still fed from the holy offerings. The same Law commanded care for the blind and counted wrongs against them as breaches of the covenant. Both facts stand behind this scene of blind people healed inside the Temple courts.
the-temple.source: International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915), entry "Blindness"; Leviticus 19:14, 21:18-22; Deuteronomy 27:18.

crowds-by-the-sea.text: Edersheim places this scene, and the feeding of the four thousand that follows it, on the eastern side of the lake in the Decapolis, among people who were not strictly Jewish. Matthew says only that Jesus came to the Sea of Galilee and went up a mountain, and other commentators put it on the western shore.
crowds-by-the-sea.source: Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book III, chapter XXXVI.

crowds-by-the-sea.text: Matthew Henry noticed that the people "brought their sick relations and friends along with them, and cast them down at Jesus' feet," and that "we read not of any thing they said to him": their condition spoke for them. Every blind person on that mountainside had been carried or led up it by someone.
crowds-by-the-sea.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1721), on Matthew 15.

answer-to-john.text: John sent his question from prison. Josephus says Herod, fearing John's hold on the people, sent him as a prisoner to the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea, and later had him killed there. Edersheim describes the place as a frontier stronghold on sheer cliffs, built by Alexander Jannaeus and enlarged by Herod the Great.
answer-to-john.source: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews (Whiston translation), Book XVIII, chapter 5; Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book III, chapter XXVIII.

answer-to-john.text: Opening the eyes of the blind was understood as a mark of the Messiah. Smith's calls it "a peculiar attribute" of the promised one in Isaiah 29:18 and 42:7, and Jesus's answer to John begins with the words of Isaiah 35:5. He was answering a question about who He was with the people He had healed.
answer-to-john.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entry "Blindness"; Isaiah 29:18, 35:5, 42:7.

pool-of-bethesda.text: The pool was in the north of the city near the Sheep Gate, where the road came in from the Mount of Olives, Bethany and Jericho. The site identified today lies beside the Church of St. Anne, near the gate now called the Lions' Gate, and was excavated in the 19th century.
pool-of-bethesda.source: Wikipedia, "Pool of Bethesda," revision of 22 July 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0); Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book III, chapter XII.

pool-of-bethesda.text: It began in the eighth century BC as a reservoir made by damming a small valley, and a second pool was added about 200 BC. The excavated pools are some thirteen metres deep, which is why the old idea that sheep were washed there is now thought unlikely. In the century before Jesus, caves beside the pools were made into small baths used for healing or religion, and some scholars think the crowd of sick people in John 5 reflects a place already known for cures.
pool-of-bethesda.source: Wikipedia, "Pool of Bethesda," revision of 22 July 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0).
pool-of-bethesda.caution: The link to a healing shrine is the article's suggestion, not a settled fact.

pool-of-bethesda.text: Matthew Henry read the covered walkways as a place where human charity met God's mercy: "nature has provided remedies, but men must provide hospitals." He thought the blind, the lame and the paralyzed were named because, being least able to get themselves into the water, they waited longest.
pool-of-bethesda.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1721), on John 5.

pool-of-bethesda.text: The name probably means "house of mercy" or "house of grace." Edersheim, in 1883, admitted that every attempt to explain it had failed; the modern view rests on Hebrew and Aramaic roots and fits a place where the sick gathered hoping for healing.
pool-of-bethesda.source: Wikipedia, "Pool of Bethesda," revision of 22 July 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0); Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book III, chapter XII.

the-banquet.text: A formal meal in Jesus's day was taken after sunset, with guests reclining on couches set around three sides of a square, the fourth side left open for the servants, and a shared dish into which each guest dipped. For a great feast the guests were invited beforehand, and a second summons went out on the day when the meal was ready; places were set by rank. Edersheim cites a rabbinic saying that no one in Jerusalem went to a feast until the invitation had been given and repeated. That is why, in the parable, the excuses come when the servant announces that all is ready.
the-banquet.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entry "Meals"; Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book V, chapter V.

the-banquet.text: The scene is a Sabbath meal at a leading Pharisee's house, just after Jesus healed a man with dropsy in front of the guests and watched them choose the best places. When Jesus spoke of feasting the poor, a guest answered with the common hope of a great feast at the coming of God's kingdom, and the parable was told in reply to him.
the-banquet.source: Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book IV, chapter XVI; Luke 14:1-15.

the-banquet.text: Edersheim reads the three invitations as widening circles: first the leading people of the city, who make excuses; then the poor, crippled, blind and lame from the city's streets and lanes; then people outside the city altogether, on the highways and under the hedges. "Compel them to come in" he takes as earnest, pressing invitation, not force, since such guests would hardly believe they were wanted. Matthew Henry reads the same groups as the outcasts of Israel and then the Gentiles.
the-banquet.source: Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book IV, chapter XVI; Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1721), on Luke 14.

the-banquet.text: Inviting the poor to a feast was not a new idea. The Law already required that the poor, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow share in the festival meals (Deuteronomy 14:29, 26:12), and Smith's notes the poor "were also invited to feasts." Jesus was pressing a command His hearers knew.
the-banquet.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entry "Beggar, Begging"; Deuteronomy 14:29, 26:12.

the-banquet.text: What was Jesus teaching? Both commentators on the shelf read the first saying as a rebuke of hospitality that expects repayment, and the parable as a warning that those first invited to God's kingdom were refusing it while the people nobody invited were being gathered in. Neither treats the passage as being about blind people as such; the blind stand here with the poor, the crippled and the lame as the guests God wants at His table. Matthew Henry adds that the gospel has often had its greatest success among "the maimed, and the halt, and the blind."
the-banquet.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1721), on Luke 14; Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (1883), Book IV, chapter XVI.

the-return.text: Jeremiah 30 to 33 is often called the Book of Comfort. The 1915 encyclopedia notes that Jeremiah's promises of restoration grew more frequent during and after the siege of Jerusalem, when the city's fall was certain. Matthew Henry dates this chapter to about 594 BC and heads it "Joyful Return from Captivity."
the-return.source: International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915), entry "Jeremiah"; Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1721), on Jeremiah 31.

the-return.text: Matthew Henry takes the blind and the lame in verse 8 as real travellers on a real road, and notices that God names the people least fit for a long journey as the ones He will bring. He expects two kinds of help on the way: companions who will be "eyes to the blind and legs to the lame," and God Himself as guide. The companions are Henry's addition; verse 9 names only God.
the-return.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1721), on Jeremiah 31; compare Job 29:15.

the-return.text: Henry reads verse 9 as an answer to each danger of the road home: if the country is dry, streams of water; if there is no track, a straight way they cannot miss; if the ground is rough, they will not stumble. He also draws a lesson that the blind and lame did not plead their condition as an excuse. That last point is a preacher's, and a blind reader may hear it differently from how he meant it.
the-return.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1721), on Jeremiah 31.
the-return.caution: Henry's 'do not plead inability' is his own application; flagged for Brian.

job.text: Job did his work of justice in public. Matthew Henry notes that he went out through the city to the gate, where judgment was given, and Smith's confirms that the gates of eastern cities were the places of public business and law. Smith's places Job in the land of Uz, south or south-east of Palestine, as a chieftain of great wealth and rank.
job.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1721), on Job 29; Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entries "Gate" and "Job."

job.text: Brian asked whether anyone has thought about what it means to be someone's eyes rather than to give them alms. The shelf has one writer who does. Matthew Henry reads "eyes to the blind" as counsel for people who did not know what to do, and "feet to the lame" as practical help for those who knew what to do but could not do it; and he adds that we help people best in the very thing they lack.
job.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1721), on Job 29.

job.text: Henry draws the sharper line in his comment on Matthew 9. Job, he says, was eyes to the blind, standing in for their eyes, but "he could not give eyes to the blind"; opening blind eyes is God's own work. Serving as someone's eyes and giving someone sight are different things, and Scripture names only the second as God's prerogative. The first is what a neighbour can do.
job.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1721), on Matthew 9.

job.text: Henry uses Job's phrase again when the blind and lame come home from exile in Jeremiah 31: their companions will be eyes to the blind and legs to the lame, as fellow travellers ought to be to one another. He consistently treats being someone's eyes as a service between equals on a journey, not as charity handed down.
job.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1721), on Jeremiah 31 and Proverbs 1.

job.text: Job's claim stands beside the Law's commands: do not put a stumbling block before the blind (Leviticus 19:14), and cursed is the one who leads a blind man astray (Deuteronomy 27:18). Both the 1915 encyclopedia and Smith's note that the Law specially charged Israel to care for the blind. Job describes himself as keeping that charge and going beyond it. No source on the shelf discusses the Hebrew of the verse.
job.source: International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915), entry "Blindness"; Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entry "Blindness."

jabesh-gilead.text: Jabesh-gilead lay east of the Jordan in the hills of Gilead; Smith's reports an ancient writer placing it six miles from Pella on the road to Gerasa, where the name survives in a valley called Wady Yabes. The exact site is still uncertain. Saul's first act as king was to rescue it.
jabesh-gilead.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entry "Jabesh"; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915), entry "Jabesh-gilead."

jabesh-gilead.text: Josephus explains the threat as military policy: Nahash put out the right eyes of those he conquered so that, with the left eye covered by a shield, they would be useless in battle. The Bible gives no reason beyond disgrace. Either way, the point was to make a whole town helpless and ashamed.
jabesh-gilead.source: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews (Whiston translation), Book VI, chapter 5; 1 Samuel 11:2.

jabesh-gilead.text: Smith's lists this threat with the blinding of Zedekiah as the two places where Scripture alludes to blinding on purpose for political ends.

the-jebusite-taunt.text: Josephus took the verse literally. In his telling the Jebusites shut their gates and set the blind, the lame and the maimed on the wall to mock David, saying that even they could keep him out, and trusted in the strength of their walls. His translator Whiston defended that reading in a note. Modern readers take the verse in several ways, and this is one of them.
the-jebusite-taunt.source: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews (Whiston translation), Book VII, chapter 3, with Whiston's note.

the-jebusite-taunt.text: Jebus was the old name of Jerusalem, "the city of the Jebusites." Smith's traces them to a son of Canaan and notes that they held their citadel until David took it. The 1915 encyclopedia observes that in the lists of the peoples of Canaan the Jebusites always come last, probably because they were few.
the-jebusite-taunt.source: Smith's Bible Dictionary (1884 edition), entry "Jebus"; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915), entry "Jebusite."

man-born-blind.text: How far did he walk? The modern figures, as Wikipedia reports them from an Israeli guide, put the pool at about 625 metres above sea level and the Temple Mount at about 740, a drop of some 115 metres over a straight-line distance of about 634 metres. The pool was the lowest place in the city. A blind man with mud on his eyes went down that slope through the streets, and came back up it seeing.
man-born-blind.source: Wikipedia, "Pool of Siloam," revision of 20 June 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0), citing an Israeli guide of 1980.
man-born-blind.caution: Straight-line distance; the walking route would have been longer.

man-born-blind.text: The ground between the Temple and the pool is a valley. Josephus describes the Valley of the Cheesemongers running between the upper and lower city down to Siloam, with steep slopes on either side. Excavators have reported a stepped and tiled street running from near the Temple Mount down to the pool, which they take to be the way worshippers used between the two.
man-born-blind.source: Josephus, The Wars of the Jews (Whiston translation), Book V, chapter 4; Wikipedia, "Pool of Siloam," revision of 20 June 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0), quoting a Jerusalem Post report of 26 January 2006.

man-born-blind.text: At the end of the walk there were steps. Excavators in the 1880s recorded a stairway of 34 rock-cut steps leading up from the pool's forecourt, and the pool found in 2004 has steps on at least three sides, in sets of five with landings between. For a man who could not see, the last part of the journey was a staircase down to water.
man-born-blind.source: Wikipedia, "Pool of Siloam," revision of 20 June 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0).
